analysis.title: Is America paying for China's AI?
key_insights: Syz concludes the 'US shareholders subsidise China's AI' argument is partly right but overstated: US capex does not flow to China, but it buys a technology lead that pays off for a shorter period than investors might hope.

Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta plan roughly $700bn of infrastructure spending in 2026, about 75% more than in 2025 (Financial Times). US hyperscalers are expected to pass $1tn of annual investment in 2027 (Evercore, Bank of America estimates).

Anthropic reported in February 2026 that DeepSeek, Moonshot and MiniMax generated more than 16 million exchanges with Claude through about 24,000 fraudulent accounts: MiniMax over 13 million, Moonshot over 3.4 million, DeepSeek about 150,000. The requests targeted coding, reasoning and autonomous task execution. These are company allegations and nobody has measured what the Chinese labs gained.

OpenAI made similar distillation accusations against DeepSeek in a memo to a US congressional committee in February 2026, and Google disclosed an attempt to copy Gemini using more than 100,000 prompts.

Chinese models have trailed the best US models by an average of seven months since 2023 (Epoch AI). Open-weight models in general, including US ones, trail leading closed models by a comparable margin, so the lag is not specific to China.

Chinese models rose from about 1% of OpenRouter usage in late 2024 to about 46% by mid-2026, driven by price: OpenRouter finds them 60% to 90% cheaper than leading US alternatives. Cursor launched a model built on Moonshot's Kimi in March 2026 without disclosing it at launch.

Chinese labs are not low-spend: Alibaba and Tencent together spent more than RMB 120bn (about $17bn) in Q2 2026, and ByteDance plans about $28bn in 2026. DeepSeek's $5.6mn figure covered only the final training run, while SemiAnalysis estimated its servers alone were worth about $1.6bn.

Ideas flow both ways: DeepSeek developed and openly published several techniques for cheaper training and inference that US labs have adopted. China produced about 27% of global AI publications in 2024 against 12% for the US (CSET). US export controls on chips pushed Chinese engineers to get more out of less hardware.

Most hyperscaler spend is insulated from model copying because it funds cloud capacity, advertising systems and AI services for paying customers. Google Cloud has more than $460bn of contracted future revenue, and Meta attributed part of its 33% Q1 2026 revenue growth to AI-driven ad targeting. Only spending on developing new models is exposed.

Of 178 large open-weight models released by Chinese labs in 2026, 59% use the Apache 2.0 licence and 22% the MIT licence, both allowing free commercial use. Global developers and US start-ups are the main beneficiaries. Andreessen Horowitz reported in 2025 that up to 80% of start-ups pitching it with open models were building on Chinese ones.

US labs are deploying detection tools that can degrade answers sent to suspected copiers. DeepSeek's 150,000 exchanges are small relative to the data needed to train a modern model, which suggests most of its progress was its own work.

US labs still capture most AI revenue: Anthropic annualised revenue passed $65bn at end of July 2026 and OpenAI's reached about $40bn, while Epoch AI estimates no other lab, Chinese included, earns more than $1bn.

The gap is narrowing: in September 2026 open-weight models handled 71.5% of traffic on Vercel's AI gateway and 23% of spending, up from under 4% in June. Anthropic's share of spending on that platform fell from 63.7% to 43.9% between August and September. The data cover a single platform.

Moonshot's Kimi K3 (released July 2026) beat Anthropic's Fable 5 on Arena's coding ranking and placed above Opus 4.8 in its general ranking. Axios reported it outperformed Anthropic's latest system on a coding test at 40% lower cost. Arena rankings are user votes on specific tasks, not independent tests, so a Chinese lead is not established.

Investment implications: the impact on large US tech groups is limited because profits depend mainly on cloud and advertising. Cheaper AI has stimulated demand, which benefits chipmakers. Pressure is more direct on frontier labs, whose pricing power is weakening in everyday applications while premium pricing holds for the most complex tasks. Anthropic and OpenAI IPO disclosures should show the effect on margins.

sector_views.rationale: Impact from cheap Chinese models is limited because profits rely on cloud services and advertising rather than exclusive access to frontier models.
Cheaper AI has stimulated demand, which benefits chipmakers.
Pricing power is weakening across everyday applications, though a premium remains for the most complex tasks. IPO disclosures should show the margin effect.

earnings_insights: Meta attributed part of its 33% revenue growth in Q1 2026 to AI-driven ad targeting (reported, via Yahoo Finance).
Google Cloud has more than $460bn of contracted future revenue (backlog, not recognised revenue).
Anthropic annualised revenue passed $65bn at the end of July 2026 and OpenAI's reached about $40bn (annualised run-rate, not reported GAAP revenue).
risk_factors: Open-weight Chinese models erode pricing power of US frontier labs in everyday applications.
Distillation may let Chinese labs close the gap faster than the seven-month historical lag; Kimi K3 rankings raise the possibility they stop trailing.
Growth in AI demand may not be sufficient to offset the decline in pricing power.
Vercel share-of-spend shift covers a single platform, so the trend may not generalise.
Arena rankings are based on user votes, not independent tests.
geopolitical: US labs allege Chinese labs DeepSeek, Moonshot and MiniMax used fraudulent accounts to distil Claude; OpenAI made similar accusations against DeepSeek to a US congressional committee.
US export controls restrict China's access to the most powerful AI chips, pushing Chinese engineers toward efficiency.
cross_bank_references: Hyperscaler 2027 investment above $1tn is based on estimates from Evercore and Bank of America.

tension_points.bull_case: The 'subsidy' argument has merit: Anthropic alleges 16 million fraudulent exchanges, Chinese open models went from about 1% to about 46% of OpenRouter usage, open-weight models took 23% of spending on Vercel's gateway, and Kimi K3 topped some Arena rankings.
tension_points.bear_case: Most hyperscaler spend funds cloud, advertising and services that copying cannot touch. Chinese labs spend heavily themselves, US labs capture most AI revenue (Anthropic over $65bn annualised), and detection tools are making copying harder.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Anthropic and OpenAI IPO disclosures showing margin pressure from pricing power erosion, or demand growth failing to offset falling prices.

theme_stances.key_argument: America's technological lead generates returns for an increasingly limited period, and the period is narrowing rapidly.
theme_stances.evidence: America's technological lead generates returns for an increasingly limited period
